questions.q: In the test-runner outline (for case in eval_set: ... grade(output, case.expected)), what is the purpose of running this loop the same way every time?
options: To make the test run faster regardless of accuracy
Because the eval set changes every time it runs
To avoid ever having to grade open-ended output
To remove the inconsistency of a human applying different judgment call to call when reviewing outputs by hand
questions.explain: Running the identical loop every time removes the variability of manual review, where a human might judge similar outputs differently from one review session to the next.

questions.q: Which grading method is best suited for checking that an output is valid JSON matching an exact expected structure?
options: LLM-as-judge rubric scoring
Exact or structural match
Human spot-check sampling
Keyword or regex assertions only
questions.explain: For output with one correct, well-defined form (like valid JSON matching a schema), a direct structural/equality check is simplest and most reliable — no judgment call needed.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say LLM-as-judge grading still needs a human spot-check in the loop?
options: Because LLM judges are never allowed to grade anything
Because human review is always faster than automated grading
Because a judge model can drift or develop blind spots over time, the same way any single evaluator can
Because LLM-as-judge only works on exact-match cases
questions.explain: The lesson explains that periodic human review of a sample of judged cases catches systematic errors an LLM judge may develop over time, which pure automation wouldn't catch on its own.

questions.q: In the test run report example ({prompt_version, cases_run, passed, pass_rate, failed_ids}), why does the lesson emphasize the failed_ids field specifically?
options: Because the failed IDs tell you exactly which cases (and what kind of failure) to actually go investigate, not just that something changed
Because pass_rate is unnecessary and should be removed
Because failed_ids replaces the need for an eval set
Because it's the only field that gets logged
questions.explain: A pass rate alone signals that something changed; the specific failed case IDs (with their categories from Lesson 18) point to exactly what broke and often why.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what is true of a prompt change that ships without being run against the eval set?
options: It is automatically considered safe since the prompt wording looks reasonable
It is tested as long as the developer read the output once
Eval sets are optional and skipping them has no real consequence
It isn't meaningfully tested — it's a change someone liked the look of
questions.explain: The lesson states directly that once an eval set exists, skipping the automated run means the change wasn't really tested, regardless of how good it looked to a reviewer.
